title: Money & Economics
description: Money and economics: recognising coins and notes, buying and change, needs and wants, earning and saving, banks and digital payments, supply and demand, markets, inflation, taxes and the economy of India — building both numeracy and economic thinking.

lessons.title: Meet the Rupee
objectives: Recognise common Indian coins and notes
Know money is exchanged for things we buy
explanation: In India, our money is called the rupee. Its symbol is ₹. We have coins (round metal pieces) and notes (paper money).
Coins include ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 and ₹10. Notes include ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100 and more. Each one has its number written on it.
We use money to buy things. At a shop, you give money and the shopkeeper gives you what you bought.

context.text: The ₹ symbol was adopted by the Government of India in 2010; it was designed by D. Udaya Kumar.

vocabulary.meaning: what we use to buy things

examples: A ₹10 coin and a ₹10 note have the same value.
Buying a banana for ₹5.

story.title: Kiko's First Purchase
story.text: Kiko held a shiny ₹5 coin. At the fruit stall, Kiko pointed to a banana. "Five rupees, please," said the fruit seller. Kiko handed over the coin and got the banana. "I bought it myself!" Kiko beamed.

lessons.title: Paying at the Shop
objectives: Compare prices to find which costs more
Pay small amounts with coins
explanation: A price tells how much something costs. A pencil might cost ₹5; a book might cost ₹50. The book is more expensive.
You can pay ₹5 with one ₹5 coin, or with a ₹2 coin, a ₹2 coin and a ₹1 coin. Different coins can add up to the same amount.
If you don't have enough money, you can't buy it yet — you might save for it.
examples: A ₹50 toy is more expensive than a ₹10 toy.

story.title: Momo's Coin Puzzle
story.text: Momo wanted a ₹5 balloon but had no ₹5 coin. Momo had two ₹2 coins and a ₹1 coin. "Two plus two is four, plus one is five!" Momo paid and floated off happily with a red balloon.

lessons.title: Need or Want?
objectives: Sort items into needs and wants
Explain why needs come first
explanation: Needs are things we must have to live and be healthy: food, water, a home, clothes, medicine and education.
Wants are things that are nice to have but we can live without: toys, sweets, games, fancy shoes.
Families have a limited amount of money, so they buy needs first and wants when there is enough left. Choosing is part of using money wisely.

vocabulary.meaning: something we must have to live

examples: Rice and dal: needs. A new video game: a want.
School books: a need. Stickers: a want.

story.title: The Shopping List
story.text: Zuri's family had ₹500 for the week. The list had rice, vegetables, milk, soap — and a toy Zuri wanted. They bought everything on the list first. Only ₹50 was left, not enough for the toy. "Next month, if we save," said Mama. Zuri understood: needs first.

activities.prompt: Which comes first when money is limited?

thinking: Can something be a need for one person and a want for another?
How does it feel to wait for a want?
speaking: Sort ten things in your home into needs and wants with a grown-up.

lessons.title: My Piggy Bank
objectives: Explain that people earn money by working
Make a plan to save for something
explanation: Money doesn't grow on trees! People earn money by working: farmers sell crops, teachers get paid salaries, shopkeepers sell goods.
When we get money, we can spend it now or save it for later. Saving means putting money away to use for something bigger.
If you want a ₹100 book and save ₹10 a week, you need 10 weeks. Saving needs patience!

vocabulary.meaning: money paid regularly for a job

examples: A potter earns money by selling pots.
Saving coins in a gullak (piggy bank).

story.title: Rangi's Gullak
story.text: Rangi wanted a ₹60 paint set. Every week, Grandpa gave Rangi ₹10 for helping in the garden. Rangi put it in a clay gullak. Week one: ₹10. Week three: ₹30. Week six: ₹60! Rangi broke open the gullak and bought the paints — and painted a picture of Grandpa.

activities.prompt: Save ₹10 each week. After 4 weeks you have…

thinking: Why do grown-ups go to work?

lessons.title: Count Your Change
objectives: Calculate change from a purchase
Check change by counting up
explanation: If something costs ₹35 and you pay with a ₹50 note, the shopkeeper gives back the difference: ₹50 − ₹35 = ₹15. This is your change.
Shopkeepers often "count up": from ₹35, add ₹5 to make ₹40, then ₹10 to make ₹50. That's ₹15.
Always check your change — mistakes happen.

vocabulary.meaning: money given back when you pay more than the price
how much more one number is than another
a paper showing what you bought and paid

examples: Price ₹72, pay ₹100, change ₹28.
Two items ₹20 + ₹15 = ₹35 total.

story.title: The Honest Shopkeeper
story.text: Ivaan bought a notebook for ₹42 and paid ₹50. The shopkeeper gave ₹18 change. Ivaan counted up: ₹42 + ₹8 = ₹50 — so the change should be ₹8! He gave ₹10 back. The shopkeeper smiled, "Thank you for your honesty — and your good maths!"

thinking: Why is counting up a useful trick?
What should you do if you get too much change?
speaking: Show a grown-up how you would work out change from ₹100 for an ₹82 item.

lessons.title: What Does a Bank Do?
objectives: Explain what banks do
Describe digital payments and basic safety
explanation: A bank keeps people's money safe. Putting money in is a deposit; taking money out is a withdrawal. Banks also lend money to people and businesses.
Banks pay a little extra money, called interest, when you keep savings with them, because they can lend that money to others.
Today many people in India pay with UPI apps on phones by scanning QR codes. Digital money still needs care: never share PINs or OTPs, and children should use digital payments only with a parent.

context.text: UPI (Unified Payments Interface) was launched in India in 2016 by the National Payments Corporation of India and is now used for billions of transactions each month.

vocabulary.meaning: a place that keeps money safe and lends money
take money out of a bank

examples: Scanning a QR code at a vegetable stall to pay.
Opening a children's savings account with a parent.

story.title: The Gullak and the Bank
story.text: Zuri's gullak was full. Grandpa took her to the bank to open a savings account. "Will they keep my money safe?" she asked. "Yes," said the bank officer, "and every year we'll add a little interest." A year later, Zuri saw her savings had grown — without her doing anything!

lessons.title: Supply and Demand
objectives: Explain how supply and demand affect prices
Use real examples like seasonal fruit
explanation: A market is where buyers and sellers meet — a vegetable market, a shop or an online store.
Supply is how much of something is available. Demand is how much people want it. When supply is high and demand low, prices tend to fall. When supply is low and demand high, prices tend to rise.
Mangoes are cheap in peak summer when there are lots of them, and expensive at the start of the season. Onion prices can jump when bad weather damages crops.

vocabulary.meaning: a place where buyers and sellers meet

examples: Flower prices rise before festivals when demand is high.
Two tea stalls side by side keep prices fair through competition.

story.title: The Mango Seller's Year
story.text: In April, Ramesh's first mangoes sold for ₹400 a dozen; few were available and everyone wanted them. By late May, mangoes were everywhere and the price fell to ₹150. "Same mangoes," he laughed, "but the market changed."

thinking: Why might flower prices rise before Diwali?

lessons.title: Costs, Revenue and Profit
objectives: Calculate cost, revenue and profit
Plan a small business
explanation: A business sells goods or services. Costs are what you spend to make them (ingredients, cups). Revenue is the money you receive from sales.
Profit = revenue − costs. If you spend ₹200 on ingredients and sell 30 cups of lemonade at ₹10, revenue is ₹300 and profit is ₹100. If costs are higher than revenue, it's a loss.
Entrepreneurs find a need, set a fair price, and keep customers happy. Social enterprises use business to solve social or environmental problems.

vocabulary.meaning: money spent to make or provide something
a person who starts a business

examples: A home tiffin service run by a neighbour.
A social enterprise making sanitary pads affordable.

story.title: The Nimbu-Pani Stall
story.text: Kiko and Zuri set up a nimbu-pani (lemonade) stall for a school fair. Lemons, sugar and cups cost ₹250. They sold 40 glasses at ₹10 each — ₹400. "Profit: ₹150!" said Zuri. They gave half to the school library fund.

activities.prompt: If costs are higher than revenue, it is a loss.

thinking: How would you decide the price of something you make?
What makes customers come back?
speaking: Pitch a small business idea to your family with costs and expected profit.

lessons.title: Why Did Prices Go Up?
objectives: Explain inflation and purchasing power
Describe how the RBI tries to control inflation
explanation: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time. When prices rise, each rupee buys less — its purchasing power falls. Your grandparents may remember a cup of tea costing a few paise!
Inflation is measured using price indexes like the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which tracks the cost of a basket of common goods and services.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) aims to keep inflation moderate (around a 4% target, within a band of 2–6%). It can raise interest rates to cool spending when inflation is high.

context.text: Under India's flexible inflation targeting framework (since 2016), the RBI targets 4% CPI inflation with a tolerance band of 2–6%.

vocabulary.meaning: a general rise in prices over time
a measure of price changes for common items
Reserve Bank of India, the central bank

examples: A ₹10 snack costing ₹12 a few years later.
Savings losing value if interest is lower than inflation.

story.title: Grandfather's Price List
story.text: Grandfather showed Ivaan an old bill from 1980: rice for a few rupees a kilo, a cinema ticket for a few rupees. Ivaan compared it with today's prices — many times higher. "Did everything get more expensive?" Ivaan asked. "Yes," said Grandfather, "but salaries rose too. That's inflation."

lessons.title: Why Do We Pay Taxes?
objectives: Explain direct and indirect taxes
Describe how taxes fund public goods
explanation: Taxes are money people and businesses pay to the government. Direct taxes, like income tax, are paid on income. Indirect taxes, like GST (Goods and Services Tax), are included in the prices of things we buy.
Governments use taxes to provide public goods and services: roads, schools, hospitals, defence, police, clean water and support for people in need.
Each year, the Union Budget, presented in Parliament, shows how the government plans to raise and spend money. Paying taxes honestly is a civic duty.

context.text: GST was introduced in India on 1 July 2017, replacing many earlier indirect taxes.

vocabulary.meaning: something provided for everyone, like streetlights

examples: GST included in the price of a notebook.
Taxes funding a new government hospital.

story.title: The Streetlight Question
story.text: Ivaan asked, "Who pays for the streetlights?" Papa explained that part of the money they paid in taxes, and in GST when shopping, went to the government, which paid for streetlights, roads and Ivaan's school building. "So we all chipped in," said Ivaan.

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: GDP and Growth
objectives: Explain GDP, growth rate and unemployment
Interpret basic economic data
explanation: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year. GDP growth rate shows how fast the economy is expanding. GDP per capita divides GDP by population.
Unemployment measures people who want work but can't find it. In India, much work is informal — without written contracts or social security — which makes measurement complex.

Countries trade: exports are goods sold abroad (like software services, pharmaceuticals and textiles from India); imports are goods bought from abroad (like crude oil). Exchange rates set how many rupees buy a dollar.

context.text: Economists debate how best to measure informal employment and wellbeing; GDP is useful but incomplete.

vocabulary.meaning: total value of goods and services produced
people seeking work who cannot find it

examples: India is a major exporter of IT services.
Crude oil is one of India's largest imports.

story.title: Two Countries, Same GDP
story.text: Two imaginary countries both have the same GDP. In one, wealth is shared and most people have good schools and hospitals; in the other, a few are very rich and most are poor. "GDP tells you the size of the cake," said the economics teacher, "not how it's shared."

activities.prompt: GDP per capita means GDP divided by…

thinking: What important things does GDP leave out?

speaking: Explain GDP growth to someone using the "size of the cake" analogy.

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: The 1991 Turning Point
objectives: Describe major phases of India's economic history
Evaluate the effects of the 1991 reforms
explanation: After independence, India followed a mixed, planned economy with Five-Year Plans, public sector industries and many controls on business (often called the "licence raj").
In 1991, facing a balance-of-payments crisis, India began liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation (LPG reforms): reducing licences, opening to foreign investment and trade.

Since then, growth has generally been faster, with a boom in IT and services and a large reduction in extreme poverty. Challenges remain: creating enough good jobs, reducing inequality, supporting agriculture and growing sustainably. Economists debate the reforms' full effects.

context.text: In 1991, India had foreign exchange reserves sufficient for only a few weeks of imports; reforms were announced in the July 1991 budget by Finance Minister Manmohan Singh.
Economists and historians differ on how to weigh the benefits and costs of liberalisation for different groups.

vocabulary.meaning: reducing government controls on the economy
transferring businesses from government to private ownership
record of a country's transactions with the world
a national economic plan for five years

examples: IT companies in Bengaluru growing rapidly after 1991.
More foreign brands available in Indian markets.

story.title: The Crisis Summer
story.text: In 1991, India had so little foreign currency that it pledged gold to borrow money. That July, the government announced sweeping reforms. A young engineer who started a software company that decade later said, "Before, getting a phone line took years. After, everything moved faster."

activities.prompt: India's major economic reforms began in…
Economists debate the full effects of the reforms.

thinking: Who gained most from the reforms, and who may have been left behind?
What economic challenge should India prioritise now?
speaking: Debate: "The 1991 reforms benefited all Indians equally." Present both sides.
